item.research_question: How does temperature influence the superplasticity, strengthening mechanisms, and deformation behavior of CoNiCrFeMn high entropy alloy nanowires compared to single-component Ag nanowires?
item.material_system: CoNiCrFeMn equiatomic high entropy alloy (20 at.% each) and single-element Ag nanowires
item.processing_route: Molecular dynamics simulations using LAMMPS; nanowires extracted from bulk FCC along [110] with circular (110) cross-section; equilibrated at 77, 300, and 1000 K; constant strain rate of 10^8 1/s applied in NVT ensemble
item.test_conditions: Tensile deformation at 77 K, 300 K, and 1000 K; strain rate 10^8 1/s; Ag NW (47,250 atoms); HEA NW (55,216 atoms)
key_findings: At 77 K, Ag NWs exhibit superplasticity via (110) to (100) cross-section reorientation driven by partial dislocation nucleation and twin boundary propagation.
CoNiCrFeMn HEA NWs reach a peak stress of ~6.2 GPa at 5–6% elongation at 77 K, showing serration behavior due to Lomer Cottrell lock formation.
At 77 K, HEA NWs achieve ~45% elongation to fracture due to synergistic TWIP (twinning induced plasticity) and TRIP (transformation induced plasticity) mechanisms.
At 300 K, HEA NWs maintain a flow stress of ~5.5 GPa at 5% strain with simultaneous partial dislocation nucleation and deformation twinning.
At 1000 K, HEA NWs maintain good flow stress and ductility, with FCC-HCP martensitic transformation dominating and HCP phase fraction increasing rapidly.
Dislocation density is highest at 77 K and decreases with increasing temperature, shifting the dominant mechanism from TWIP to TRIP.
Lomer Cottrell locks in HEA NWs act as barriers at low temperatures but are unlocked/annihilated by HCP phase formation at high temperatures.
item.mechanism: The exceptional strength-ductility trade-off in HEA nanowires arises from the synergistic interaction of twinning induced plasticity (TWIP), transformation induced plasticity (TRIP) via FCC-HCP martensitic transformation, and cross-section reorientation. At low temperatures, lattice distortion and friction hinder partial dislocation motion, promoting Lomer Cottrell lock formation which enhances work hardening. At high temperatures, thermal energy facilitates the unlocking of these locks via HCP phase accumulation, enabling continued plasticity and refractory properties.
item.limitations: The study is based on molecular dynamics simulations with a specific strain rate (10^8 1/s) and does not account for experimental synthesis challenges or long-term stability under different strain rates.
item.future_work: The findings could be useful for designing nanowires at different temperatures with high stability and superior mechanical properties in the semiconductor industry.
quotes: HEA nanowires can perform exceptional strength-ductility trade-offs at cryogenic temperatures.
Simultaneous activation of twining induced plasticity and transformation induced plasticity are responsible for the plasticity at different stages and temperatures.
The good refractory property of the HEA NW in this work is attributed to the same synergistic mechanism as the aforementioned one.
